message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What You’re Generally Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |----------|-----------------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a security deposit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Keep a written move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs that affect health or safety must be made promptly. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or letter) and give a reasonable time to fix the issue.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may:
 – Withhold rent (after following the proper notice procedure).
 – Make the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent (Texas Property Code §92.006).
 – File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Entry & Privacy** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable” means a time that is convenient for both parties. | • Keep a log of all entry notices.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry and document the incident. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• Tenants who sign a fixed‑term lease must honor the term unless the landlord breaches the lease. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Eviction** | • Landlord must follow the **Texas Property Code §92.001** eviction process: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a **motion to dismiss** in the county court. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent (up to the amount of the repair). | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the repair and deduction. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report disturbances (e.g., noise, harassment) to the landlord in writing. | | **Fair Housing** | • Landlords must comply with federal and state fair housing laws. | • Report violations to HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas offers free or low‑cost legal aid for tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar association referral services). | • Contact a local tenant‑rights group or legal aid clinic. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Note any clauses about rent, repairs, entry, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month termination, 3‑day notice for non‑payment. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Write a clear, dated notice to the landlord and keep a copy. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If the landlord is unresponsive, contact TDHCA, HUD, or a local tenant‑rights organization. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, housing code enforcement | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair housing complaints, tenant rights information | https://www.hud.gov | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints | https://www.tchra.texas.gov | | **Local Legal Aid** | Free or low‑cost legal representation | Search “legal aid Texas” or contact your county bar association | | **Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Advocacy, workshops, legal clinics | e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local community centers | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, fair treatment, and a clear process for ending your tenancy or addressing disputes. If you encounter problems, document everything, give proper notice, and use the available state and federal resources to protect your rights.
